The other is Book Insights, from Google Play Books. It's a Gemini-powered reading assistant that summarizes what you've read so far and lets you ask spoiler-free questions about the book. It's designed to help without interrupting your reading flow.

blocks.cap: Rakuten Kobo

blocks.x: E-book platform Rakuten Kobo rejected 45% of the submissions that came into its self-publishing platform last year.
As AI-generated books poured in all at once, Kobo tightened screening on its self-publishing service, Kobo Writing Life.
Javier Celaya says "AI is not just another incremental shift." "It touches everything publishing does — creation, curation, production, translation, marketing, distribution, and rights management."

AI literacy in publishing is rising. Many people use chatbots daily and test copywriting, proofreading, and translation tools, but few have built an AI agent to redesign a workflow or used an LLM to compare business scenarios. Knowing how to use a tool is different from understanding it, and Celaya sees this gap as the industry's biggest blind spot.

After 20 years working in publishing and creative industries, he enrolled this year in an executive master's program in AI at Spain's Instituto de Inteligencia Artificial (IIA). What he was looking for wasn't a crash course in prompting, but a real understanding of how models are built and trained, who owns the data, and where AI's limits lie.

The program changed how he approaches AI. Now, before he even opens a tool, he thinks through exactly what he wants an agent to do. He also knows what questions to ask when a vendor promises its model was "trained on clean data" or glosses over data sovereignty and reuse policies. Informed skepticism, he says, is worth more than mastering any single tool.

He says watching healthcare, automotive, pharma, and entertainment bring AI into core operations gave him a comparative lens on where they stumbled and what actually delivered value. Publishing talks about AI from a defensive posture, while other fields have already launched projects with the very tools we're still just debating.

Publishing's interest in AI stays almost entirely focused on cost-cutting. But that's the floor of what AI can do for publishing, not the ceiling. The questions that will actually define the next decade are missing: what can be fully automated, where humans need to stay, and how AI can grow publishing rather than just cut its costs.

For instance, AI translation that turns e-books and audiobooks into multiple languages could bring key titles and authors to new readers at a scale never seen before. Once language and localization stop being bottlenecks, marketing and distribution can be redrawn from local to global. The opportunity is large, but few are examining it closely.

The hardest question is whether to be a partner or an adversary to AI companies. Celaya's answer is "both." The fact that many AI companies trained on copyrighted work without consent or compensation can't be ignored, and publishers need to demand redress. Litigation and partnership negotiations aren't contradictory — they're two paths that can run at the same time.

He says AI training should be a requirement, not a recommendation, for anyone in management. Without a structural understanding of what AI can and can't do, you can't responsibly set an AI strategy for a publisher or a streaming platform.

The leaders who navigate the AI era best won't be the ones who know AI in the abstract, but the ones who understand it deeply enough to ask the right questions of their teams, their tech partners, and the models themselves.

When nearly 90% of university librarians now say they accept AI as a legitimate tool at their institution, the debate can look settled. That was the headline figure in a recent survey of 311 librarians across 31 countries. But legitimacy is not enthusiasm. Institutional acceptance does not automatically translate into individual conviction.

blocks.cap: A toy robot reading a book

blocks.x: Across regions, librarians said they are more cautious about AI than administrators or faculty. Unlike administrators focused on adoption or researchers excited about new features, librarians see both the technology's promise and its practical weaknesses.

In the United States, about 30% of respondents showed active rejection or non-use, while nearly 40% in the UK and Ireland were non-committal or negative. Skepticism was especially high in Canada. Respondents from the Middle East, Africa, India and Asia-Pacific were more pragmatic, often applying AI to specific, defined tasks.

The way AI enters universities partly explains librarians' distance from it. Campus-wide licenses often arrive bundled into existing enterprise software, so to IT departments or administrators it looks like an upgrade to a service they already use. That is why institutional acceptance moves faster than individual enthusiasm. One respondent put it this way: "It ranges from outright bans to full acceptance, department by department, and we all lean on 'academic freedom' to let professors set their own rules for students."

Trust is the central theme in how librarians approach AI. Libraries have long served as intermediaries, curating collections, verifying information sources and guiding researchers. Many librarians are uneasy with the 'black box' nature of large language models, which produce plausible results while showing almost nothing about how they got there. One respondent's comment captures that concern: "AI hallucinates and invents papers that don't exist, and when people request them, it wastes their time and ours."

Only 47% of respondents, less than half, had formal guidelines in place. A more visible problem is where responsibility lies. At many institutions, particularly in Europe, AI governance responsibility rests not with the library but with IT departments, research offices or administrators. One respondent described that fragmentation this way: "There is no one in charge, no central body leading AI efforts. It's just happening scattered across campus."

The rise of AI is both a challenge and an opportunity for librarians. Over decades, libraries have shifted from managing physical collections to supporting digital scholarship, data management and open-access publishing, and AI may be the next phase. As one respondent put it, "the consensus is that AI is a transformative tool that needs guidance, not rejection."

The implications for academic publishers are significant too. The study says what librarians most want from publishers is not direct involvement in institutional governance but transparency: clear disclosure of how publishers themselves use AI, what protections they place on content, and above all what measures they take to safeguard research integrity.

blocks.cap: Storytel Genie

blocks.x: Audiobook service Storytel is unveiling AI features that summarize chapters, hold conversations, and offer a personalized 'Top Picks' list to help listeners choose what to hear next.

Storytel Genie is an AI companion that adds a layer of interaction and personalization to the audiobook experience. It reads the user's context and mood, explains why a particular book might resonate, helps choose the next story, and generates recaps when a listener loses track of the plot.

There are three features. First, 'Chat' is an interface for talking with Genie anywhere in the app to get book recommendations and more context on a specific book or author. Second, 'Recap' breaks down recent plot developments into short summaries, letting listeners jump right back into the story after missing an episode, taking a break, or dozing off mid-chapter. Third, 'Top Picks For You' offers hyper-personalized recommendations based on each listener's history and tastes, with a short description highlighting the key point of each book.

Genie is built on a book-specific agent architecture, combining advanced language models from Google Gemini, OpenAI and Anthropic with Exa's real-time knowledge capabilities. Storytel's own metadata layer anchors the AI firmly to the source material to protect intellectual property.
Chief Product and Technology Officer Johan Ståhle said, "Storytel Genie truly defines Storytel's next chapter — a shift toward a more personal, immersive and interactive book experience."
Genie rolls out first to subscribers in Sweden today and will be available across all of Sweden by July 1. Other markets will open one after another starting in August.

This is a story about China's web fiction market, as reported by Electronic Times. The free platform Fanqie Novel sharply tightened its crackdown on AI-generated content in the first half of this year. In June alone, it rejected contracts for more than 100,000 low-quality works and processed more than 40,000 works that violated its rules. It sanctioned 855 violating accounts, with some suspended permanently.

Fanqie Novel isn't blocking AI itself. It filters out writing with tangled sentences, plots that don't hold together, padding with no real content, or a lack of originality. By contrast, Qimao Chinese Network and Qidian Chinese Network have told writers that they ban any form of AI-assisted writing, in any shape.

The problem is that detection isn't perfect. Since AI was built by learning from human writing, even human-written text can be mistaken for AI style. That creates a paradox: some writers now work hard to write in a way that doesn't look like AI. They use 'humanizer' tools that turn AI-sounding sentences into a more 'human' style, and pass drafts around to each other before publishing to check for any trace of AI.

Industry observers think today's generative AI still can't fully replace a long novel on its own. A story running into the millions of characters needs to keep track of its world-building, character relationships, and prior events, and carry them forward consistently. In the end, the real question isn't whether AI was used, but how to protect quality and the value of human-made creative work.

blocks.cap: Nadim Sadek, Gvantsa Jobava, Senthil Nathan

blocks.x: The 35th International Publishers Congress, held in Kuala Lumpur, once again presented two awards honoring achievement and innovation in publishing. At the closing gala dinner, the International Publishers Association (IPA) announced that Brazilian publisher Alfredo Weiszflog would receive the 2026 IPA Champion Award. Two AI companies already well known in publishing, Shimmr and Ailaysa, took home the IPA Publishing Innovation Award.

The Champion Award goes to an individual who has gone beyond the ordinary call of duty to advance IPA's goals for the publishing industry. The IPA described Weiszflog as a central pillar of the Brazilian and international publishing markets over a half-century career.

blocks.cap: Alfredo Weiszflog

blocks.x: His publishing life began in 1967 on the marketing team at Companhia Melhoramentos, and he went on to work through nearly every department at the company. According to the IPA, the publisher modernized under his leadership and drew some of Brazil's leading authors. He served as president of the Brazilian Book Chamber (CBL) from 1985 to 1989, and organized Brazil's first appearance as guest of honor at the Frankfurt Book Fair in 1994. In a video shown at the ceremony, he said the moment fulfilled a promise he'd made to himself long ago, and that he was grateful to receive this recognition while he's still alive.
The Publishing Innovation Award goes to an organization or individual that has carried out an innovative publishing practice that others can replicate and that benefits the industry.

blocks.cap: Nadim Sadek

blocks.x: Shimmr is the company behind the world's first 'Advertising as a Service (AaaS)' platform, a subscription-based autonomous AI system designed to run book marketing continuously at an affordable cost. CEO Nadim Sadek said the IPA's recognition was "deeply appreciated" by the team. He said publishing is often described as conservative and risk-averse, but their own experience was the opposite — they met broad curiosity, constructive criticism, and bold adoption, and were welcomed rather than met with suspicion, even in an era when new technology tends to draw doubt first.

Ailaysa founder and CEO Senthil Nathan also expressed thanks. He said the award means everything to a company built by people who have spent their lives among translators, writers, and publishers. He added that Ailaysa exists to make sure a book, no matter who wrote it or in what language, can reach readers anywhere in the world in the language they choose.

Ailaysa is a multilingual AI company that offers dedicated solutions for publishers, and it also created the reading and book-discovery platform Chai Reader. The IPA holds the International Publishers Congress every two years. This year's Kuala Lumpur congress ran from July 5 to 9.

The news comes from Michael Kozlowski at Good e-Reader. Reading a series on and off tends to leave the plot and characters fuzzy. Kindle's Recaps feature fills that gap, and it's now available in web browsers too.

Recaps works like a TV show's 'previously on' segment. It gives a short, spoiler-free summary of earlier books in a series or of the book you're currently reading, so you can catch up on characters and events without rereading. Until now it was only available on Kindle e-readers and the iOS app; now that content shows up in browsers as well.

Just hit 'View Recaps' on a series page on Amazon's website. Signing in with an Amazon account also shows your reading goals and history for the year. You can use whichever browser you like — Chrome, Firefox, Edge — but for now it's only open to users in the US.

Publishing industry analyst Jane Friedman led her newsletter with this research. It analyzed 500,000 anonymized English-language ChatGPT conversations to look at how people use AI to make fiction. What stood out was a small group of heavy users dubbed 'infinite story demanders,' who mass-produce repetitive AI fan fiction and erotica purely for their own private enjoyment.

Friedman highlighted the questions the study raises about AI's relationship with entertainment: "LLMs clearly enable interaction, play, and variation in ways that give users pleasure, and that raises questions about where AI fits into the contemporary storytelling and entertainment ecosystem."

The study sees AI-generated fiction as resembling an on-demand, personalized, repetitive cultural form, a sign that story consumption is starting to happen outside the paths of traditional publishing. The paper is available on arXiv.

Publishers Weekly carried this report from the 35th International Publishers Association (IPA) Congress. Running July 5-9 at the Grand Hyatt in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, the congress drew 500 people from 40 countries, with 70 speakers from six continents on stage. From the opening remarks through the keynotes and panel discussions, AI ran across the entire agenda.

Sheikh Faisal Sheikh Mansor, president of the Malaysian Book Publishers Association, opened the event by saying, "The world has changed dramatically, but our purpose of connecting people through knowledge, ideas, and stories remains the same." IPA President Gvantsa Jobava went a step further: "Our collective work has become the best source of training data for AI. If AI ever lives up to its promise, it will be solely thanks to the quality of the books all of us make."

Thad McIlroy of 'The Future of Publishing' assessed that publishing has moved past the stage of marveling at AI and into a stage asking, 'now what do we actually do?' His observation was that academic publishing is largely working to understand AI and figure out how to integrate it, while book publishing has just moved from anxiety, fear, and panic toward cautiously, and sometimes quietly, experimenting with AI.

AI wasn't the only thing on stage. Richard Mollet of RELX moderated an ethics panel, and UN Under-Secretary-General Melissa Fleming addressed the problem of disinformation and possible solutions. Kai Zenner of the European Parliament covered policy challenges, and there were also stories from Prix Voltaire winners, who have been honored for championing freedom to publish.

This is a report on the Publishers Licensing Services (PLS) conference, carried by Melina Spanoudi of The Bookseller. At the event, publishers said they're still waiting for a 'clear' legal answer on AI training, output, and licensing. The assessment was that years of copyright litigation have failed to answer the core questions publishers actually need answered before they can set an AI licensing strategy.

There's a reason for the frustration. Litigation is still ongoing in the US this year. Last May, five publishers—Elsevier, Cengage, Hachette, Macmillan, and McGraw Hill—filed a class action against Meta together with bestselling author Scott Turow. Across different courts, arguments are playing out over training data, output, licensing, and piracy, with a growing body of rulings treating model training as transformative use, even as output claims face tightening demands to prove substantial similarity to a plaintiff's own work.

PLS is the organization that launched a collective AI licensing scheme at the London Book Fair earlier this year, and around 250 UK publishers have recently said they want to take part. Licensing practice has already started moving even while everyone waits for litigation to set the standards. The full article is available to Bookseller subscribers.

The first time AI came up at a writing and publishing event, one fan fiction author got heated during the Q&A. Her argument was that the technology amounts to mass copyright infringement, trained on fan fiction sites without permission. That's a fair point, though it's an awkward one to raise given that fan fiction itself is written without the original copyright holder's permission, which could itself be infringement. Since then, it's become clear that the fan fiction community runs especially strong on anti-AI sentiment, but as in other corners of publishing, it seemed reasonable to assume quite a few people there were using AI without disclosing it.

A X user known only as John Doe found that fan fiction copied from Claude and pasted into Archive of Our Own (AO3) carries code pointing to AI involvement. Popular works inspired by 'Heated Rivalry,' 'Stranger Things' and 'The Pit' were among those flagged as having AI's hand in them.

The interesting part is the psychology. A good number of the flagged AO3 works carried an 'AI-free' tag or made strong anti-AI statements. The author keeps repeating in writing communities that "transparency and honesty around AI use can't be relied on." The honor system doesn't work, and no publisher or group with an anti-AI policy can really enforce that purity.

Audiobook publisher Bolinda has used AI to bring back the voice of the late romance author Barbara Cartland. Interviews, archival material and human input were combined to give her distinctive narration to new audiobook editions.
Rebecca Herrmann, Elise Pulford-Moore and Tara Parker told The Bookseller how they wove together AI and archives to 'clone' Cartland's voice.
The original article is behind a paywall for paying subscribers only, so details such as which titles will come out and when could not be confirmed.
Popular fiction magazine Take a Break's Fiction Feast reportedly told its regular contributing writers that it will use "AI tools" on stories produced in-house going forward.

For a magazine that has long run short fiction aimed at a mass audience, it's a signal of a shift in how stories get made, and no small change for the contributing writers and editors who've steadily supplied copy.
Details such as the specific scope of use or how writers have reacted couldn't be confirmed, as they're locked behind a paywalled article.

Three companies leading with AI data analysis are knocking on publishers' doors this year. Each targets a different angle, rights acquisition or marketing, but the pitch is similar: they'll back up decisions long made on gut feeling with data, without replacing an editor's judgment, they all say.

Spain's Alegría is about to launch 'Publisher OS,' which expands its editing tools into rights, royalties and financial management. It started as a proofreading tool and has grown to include translation, analytics, automated marketing and press release production. It counts publishers like Anagrama and Trotta as clients, has expanded into Mexico and Argentina, and has entered pilot runs with large English-language publishers. Content lead Antonio J. Rodríguez named big AI labs like OpenAI and Google, not DeepL or Grammarly, as the real competition.

Germany's Lit-X focuses on spotting books trending worldwide and connecting them through licensing. It scans 12,800 book influencers and 2.5 million posts across Amazon, Goodreads, TikTok, Instagram and YouTube, combining ratings with reach and engagement into a 'Trend Momentum' score. Editors get the results through a biweekly digest email. Instead of charging per seat, it takes flat enterprise subscriptions; co-founder Lars Leibsohn said, 'If you charge per license, nobody uses it.'

New Zealand's Narrative Muse runs a consumer recommendation engine spanning books, film and TV alongside a reader analytics dashboard for publishers and self-published authors. Drawing on taste data from roughly 100,000 users of its recommendation engine, it helps gauge reader demand at the rights and editing stage rather than only looking at sales after publication. It breaks down a single book into more than 220 attributes to match against reader taste. Co-founder Bruff Johnson said, 'We look at everything we do through an ethics lens,' calling that their edge.

This piece is from The Verge's weekly newsletter Lowpass by Janko Roettgers. Mark DeBevoise, who became OverDrive's CEO last week, says, "AI is a new frontier for us." OverDrive runs Libby, the e-book lending app used by tens of thousands of public libraries, and it now stands right where a wave of AI-made books is pouring in.

That's why Libby is getting AI content controls, a feature letting readers choose in app settings whether to see AI-generated content. It filters not just AI-written books but AI-narrated audiobooks, machine translations and AI-generated art. DeBevoise said, "we need to let people know what's there and how it was made." Libby faced backlash last year after adding its own AI recommendation feature, so OverDrive is aiming for a middle ground: letting readers and librarians avoid AI while still keeping benefits like recommendations and localization.

Founded 40 years ago to move books onto floppy disks and CD-ROMs, the company now works with 92,000 libraries, schools and universities across 115 countries. Libby's catalog holds more than 6 million books and has passed 1 billion checkouts. DeBevoise flatly says most of the catalog has nothing to do with AI, since "books from before 2020 or 2022 are, by definition, not AI."

Still, this setup may not last. Amazon has capped self-publishing uploads since 2023, and Kobo CEO Michael Tamblyn said last month that it rejects nearly half of new self-published titles over AI concerns. OverDrive has no direct channel for authors to upload books themselves, but it receives books through intermediaries like Draft2Digital, which allows AI books if they've been sufficiently edited by a person. That means AI books are hard to keep from flowing into Libby. Even so, OverDrive chose to rely on publishers self-labeling with standard metadata rather than using an AI detector.

Audiobooks make up 15% of the catalog but account for half of app usage. DeBevoise values audiobooks read by human narrators more highly, but believes translating into dozens or even a hundred languages isn't affordable without AI. Critics also say machine translation of literary works is problematic. The new filter does have an option to exclude machine translations, but it only works if the book is properly labeled.

Sudowrite rolled out a bundle of updates in its June 30 changelog. The centerpiece is Claude Sonnet 5. Anthropic had just released the new model, and Sudowrite added support right away, describing it as approaching the quality of its flagship, Opus 4.8, while following instructions noticeably well. It works across Write, Draft and plugins generally, and credit costs are actually lower.

Folder export also arrived. From the folder menu, you can now bundle an entire folder of documents into a .zip file or pull them together into a single combined .docx, making it easier to move manuscripts and materials around.

Document reordering can now be done entirely with the keyboard. The Alt (Option) key plus arrow keys change order and nest items as sub-items, with an announcement on every move that works with screen readers.

Smaller fixes followed too. These include mobile app stability (2026.26.16), preserved Write Guidance prompts, a fix for a browser tab error, optimized comment loading, preserved display of feedback text, expanded series chat history, a Quick Edit layout, adjusted draft-generation credits, and improved character detection in novel imports. The post closes with a call for beta testers for an upcoming style guide feature.

This is the lead item Carlo Carrenho flagged in Publishing Perspectives' weekly international publishing briefing. According to a Börsenblatt report citing investigations by German public broadcaster SWR and Swiss public broadcaster SRF, US AI companies are buying up large quantities of used German-language books to train large language models.

Secondhand bookshops across Germany have seen unusually large orders from the Canadian-American company Zoom Books. The orders concentrated on nonfiction and specialist titles from the 1970s onward that carry ISBNs, and the purchased books are reportedly scanned and then discarded.

Roger Sonnewald, a bookseller in Tübingen, told SWR that the purchases themselves are legal, but warned that if the discarding is true, cultural heritage could be lost. SRF reported that as freely scrapable text online runs dry, AI companies are turning to older specialist books. Some companies reportedly see buying physical books, scanning them and disposing of them as a way to lean on the US fair use doctrine.

Carrenho noted that there have been earlier reports of AI companies amassing large quantities of paper books inside the US, but this appears to be a case of the practice spreading into a foreign-language market. In the focus on out-of-print used books, he reads a sign that AI companies are now searching beyond current publishing catalogs for training material. If confirmed, he wrote, it's a trend the publishing industry needs to watch.

On the 1st, Naver Webtoon unveiled byUs, an AI storychat service built on webtoon IP. It uses official IP approved by the original creators as is, letting users become the protagonist of the story and continue their own narrative by talking with characters. The original world is respected, while the immersion is left in users' hands.

There are two ways to use it. 'Original Story' opens with an intro set in the original world and unfolds a new narrative through back-and-forth dialogue with characters. 'Fan Story' is a mode that brings in original characters to enjoy created stories with new situations and relationships. A UGC tool that lets users create and share their own Fan Stories is also provided.

Features such as suggested replies, autoplay, snapshots and special cuts add to the immersion. The first title available on byUs is 'Job Change Log.' Naver Webtoon plans to expand its IP lineup starting with titles that have a strong fan base.

Kim Shin-hyung, head of Naver Webtoon's IP business, said, "Webtoons are moving beyond content you simply 'watch' into an 'interactive' space where fans directly take part in and expand the story world." He added, "Through byUs, we will help fans rediscover the appeal of the original works and build a virtuous cycle that leads to deeper attachment to IP and a stronger lifecycle."

How do kids used to video and short-form content read? According to the National Library for Children and Young Adults' '2025 Survey on Reading and Library Use by Children and Young Adults,' use of video, e-books and audiobooks has grown compared with 2012, and young people are increasingly moving away from paper books toward digital reading on mobile devices as their main way of reading. In step with this shift, Mirae N has released reading content through its AI-based learning platform Choco.

Choco is an online platform that draws on Mirae N's 78 years of education experience to deliver content matched to each learner's level and progress. It covers curricula from early childhood through every grade of elementary school and works on PC, tablet or smartphone. In Mirae N's own 2025 parent survey, it recorded a 98% satisfaction rate. The platform also offers ChocoPop, which covers Korean, math, social studies and science, along with the AI-powered literacy, math and English services Daldal Dokhae, Daldal Suhak and Daldal Yeongeo.

Daldal Dokhae, the literacy service, runs a diagnostic test to check a student's reading disposition and level before giving personalized passages. It moves through three stages—Vocabulary Check, Reading Growth and Skill Boost—to build vocabulary and background knowledge, then on to passage comprehension and problem solving. It holds more than 2,300 passages across six fields: humanities, social studies, science, technology, art and literature. It was developed jointly by Mirae N and the Natmal Vocabulary Information Processing Institute, which created the 'LQ Literacy Test' taken by more than 240,000 people.

ChocoToon is a digital learning webtoon made by Mirae N, the top publisher of textbooks by print volume. It has digitized more than 1,000 popular educational comics and added a reward structure that links learning and reading, rather than making it just a webtoon to watch. A Mirae N representative said, "It's designed so students use their ChocoChip learning mileage points to read ChocoToon for free, leading them toward self-directed learning," adding, "Various features support a proper reading experience even in a digital environment."

Kobo said it will roll out features in the second half of 2026 that fundamentally change how its devices handle reading and writing. In a recent email to customers, CEO Michael Tamblyn previewed "development that will fundamentally change how we read and write on our devices." The timing is expected to be this fall or winter. Kobo also detailed, on its blog, changes it's making this summer.

First is StoryGraph integration. StoryGraph is an app and website for rating and reviewing books you've read and managing reading plans and challenges; now, linking an account syncs your reading history automatically, whether you're on the Kobo app, the web reader or an e-reader. There's no more need to keep track of it separately across devices. Kobo.com's product detail pages also got reorganized information and faster loading.

The web reader got attention too. New fade and swipe page-turn effects were added, alongside the existing default flicker. A feature to select and copy sentences from a book you're reading was also added, letting you pull up to 600 characters at a time.

The subscription service Kobo Plus expanded to Poland, Romania, the Czech Republic, the Philippines, Greece and Luxembourg. Users in Belgium can also pay with Bancontact, a payment method widely used there.

This is an essay by Brian Charles published in Literary Hub. Prompted by Oxford World's Classics' new translation of Proust's 'In Search of Lost Time,' it looks squarely at how AI is quietly seeping into literary translation. To Charles, translation seemed like slow, deliberate work done 'outside of time,' a poor fit for machine translation from the start. So he asked two translators who actually use the tools.

Andrew Rothwell, who translated 'The Captive,' uses Wordscope, a translation platform that brings DeepL, Google Translate and ChatGPT together on one screen. Placing the original text, the 1929 Moncrieff translation and AI's suggestions side by side cuts down on switching between screens, easing the translator's 'cognitive load,' he explains. Still, he draws a line: the decision is always his, and the machine only proposes. He does his final polishing in a Word document outside the CAT tool. He added that today's skepticism resembles the suspicion once aimed at word processors.

Sam Taylor, who won the Scott Moncrieff Prize, translates 4,000 words a day with a French PDF open on the left and Word on the right. Instead of letting ChatGPT write sentences, he uses it only for research and checking facts. He said the tool is "like working with a smart but lazy child. You can't leave it unsupervised." He recounted an episode where he asked it to research something and it invented a book title that didn't exist, then apologized. His conclusion is clear: "It holds every language on earth at its fingertips, but it has no aesthetic sense."

The numbers are telling too. A 2024 survey by the European Council of Literary Translators' Associations found overwhelmingly negative views of machine translation, and a 2025 study named translators as the profession most threatened by the spread of AI. Taylor predicted that ordinary translators would disappear, leaving only those with a distinct style. Charles wrote that his conversations with the two left him somewhat reassured, though not entirely free of unease, and that he would keep turning pages, savoring language through slow reading.

This is an essay by Rakuten Kobo CEO Michael Tamblyn for Publishing Perspectives. At a recent Kobo leadership meeting, colleagues who rarely argue had a heated debate over whether AI-generated books should be sold in the Kobo store.

Kobo receives thousands of new titles every day, and books that look AI-made keep increasing. Watching the uproar over Hachette canceling the release of Mia Ballard's buzzy novel 'Shy Girl,' Kobo's teams tried to set standards for which books to accept and which to block.

The debate actually had three strands: how much AI should be allowed in books, how to enforce any rule that is made, and what kind of bookstore Kobo wants to be in the AI era. Last year Kobo rejected 45% of the books submitted to its self-publishing platform Kobo Writing Life — literally hundreds of thousands of titles — mostly low-quality books judged to be AI-generated. Those cases are easy calls. The problem is the vast middle ground in between. Nonfiction writers use AI to organize research, and some writers ask AI for five versions of a stuck paragraph. Editors at understaffed small publishers use AI to check spelling and grammar.

Tamblyn sums up the core of the debate this way: in books, is AI plutonium or salt? Plutonium is lethal even in trace amounts, while salt, used in moderation, makes food better. Is any trace of it, like plagiarism, instant disqualification, or is it a tool that can be used with restraint? For many working writers angry at AI services trained on pirated books, AI is plutonium. But allowing only 0% AI would also filter out countless books that deserve to be read.

Enforcement is even trickier. As models improve, detecting AI-written text gets harder, and the detection software Kobo tested often misjudged human writing as AI and AI writing as human. It is too risky to let software make a call that could ruin a writer's career. A recent study in a linguistics journal found that people who regularly work with AI text judge it far better than detection software does.

The final issue was one of values: a 'readers first' view that any good book readers want should be sold, versus a 'book community first' view that the ecosystem of writers, publishers and editors must be protected — and Kobo leaned toward the latter. Everyone agreed that the book industry exists because people spend time and money on words on a page. This essay is adapted from Tamblyn's keynote at the Frankfurter Buchmesse CONTEC event, held April 21 at the Buenos Aires International Book Fair.

This is a piece by Elena Vicario, research ethics director at Frontiers, published on Scholarly Kitchen. As recent discussions of paper mills and industrialized research misconduct show, AI has become a tool that accelerates fraud at scale. But Vicario's conclusion points the other way: if AI is part of the problem, it must also be part of the solution.

Publishers already use AI-based systems to screen for image manipulation, plagiarism, signs of paper mills, and citation anomalies, with STM's Integrity Hub as a leading example. From a research ethics standpoint, whether AI belongs in academic publishing is no longer the question; what remains is how to govern it.

Peer review alone remains a contested zone. Since it handles unpublished manuscripts, concerns about security and misuse are legitimate, but with AI embedded throughout the publishing process, it's getting harder to impose a blanket ban on reviewers alone. Reviewers are already quietly using AI to summarize manuscripts, check statistics, scrutinize code, and polish sentences. The author's diagnosis is that a ban doesn't eliminate this use — it just pushes it outside regulation, out of sight.

Peer review itself has hit its limits. Submissions are rising while reviewer capacity falls behind. IOP Publishing's 'State of Peer Review 2024,' with responses from more than 3,000 researchers, named reviewer fatigue and workload concentration as structural problems.

The author proposes that the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) lead practical standards that move beyond the binary of 'allow or ban.' Five of them: meaningful disclosure of AI use; a principle that responsibility for judgment rests with the human reviewer regardless of which tool is used; a boundary where AI can help with summaries, wording, and structure but cannot replace judgments of novelty and scientific rigor; security that keeps unpublished manuscripts off substandard tools; and editorial processes that make AI use reviewable and auditable.

The wheels are already turning: STM's AI disclosure policy is set to be discussed at the 2026 World Conference on Research Integrity (WCRI). Left unaddressed, the gap between policy and reality will only widen, and AI in peer review won't disappear — it will just remain inconsistent. The piece's core point is that this gap is exactly what erodes trust.

Amazon has added new language pairs to Kindle Translate. The AI translation service, still in beta, connects KDP (Kindle Direct Publishing) authors' ebooks with readers worldwide. This expansion adds support for translation between English and Spanish, German, French, Italian, and Portuguese. Historically, fewer than 5% of books on Amazon.com have appeared in more than one language, so this opens a path for authors to reach new readers and grow their income.

KDP authors in the beta create and manage the translations themselves. They just choose a language and set a price, and a few clicks produce a fully typeset translated edition. Every translation goes through automated quality and accuracy checks before publication. Authors can review it beforehand or let it publish automatically once it's ready. Translated editions can be enrolled in KDP Select, which also puts them on Kindle Unlimited.

This expansion extends Amazon KDP's push to help independent authors reach international markets and earn more. Kindle Translate offers free translations to independent authors like Diane C. She said, "Working with Kindle Translate is better, faster, and much easier than translation services I've used before." KDP author Isabel Acuña's reaction was also featured: "Trying the Kindle Translate beta showed me that self-published authors no longer have to be held back by language when reaching readers abroad."
Kindle Translate launched in November 2025 with English↔Spanish and German→English pairs. This is the first time the language lineup has been expanded significantly.

Amazon has released a software update for Kindle and Kindle Scribe. The headline feature in firmware 5.19.5 is "Story So Far." It gives you a spoiler-free recap of the plot up to where you've read, so you don't have to flip back through chapters when you return to a book you've set aside. It works across thousands of purchased or borrowed English bestsellers.

Kindle Scribe gets a few tangible improvements. On ebooks and Word documents with enhanced typesetting, drawing a circle now automatically tidies up annotations. Along with tapping the top-right corner while reading, you can now create a bookmark by tapping the bookmark icon on a page thumbnail in Page Flip view. Sticky notes can be moved anywhere on the page by long-pressing the icon with your finger and dragging it, or by choosing "Move Note" from the three-dot menu in the note's dialogue box or the side panel.

Story So Far rolls out to every current Amazon Kindle model. The same improvement for creating bookmarks from Page Flip view thumbnails applies as well. It comes alongside performance improvements, bug fixes, and other general refinements. Amazon has extended the AI summaries (Recaps) it introduced at the series level in 2025 to cover where you are within a single book. The piece was written by Michael Kozlowski.

This piece for The Scholarly Kitchen was co-written by chef Hong Zhou and guest blogger Adam Hyde, founder of Pure Science Inc. If agents can conjure up software on the fly, is there still a reason to rent a vendor's fixed product by the seat? That question, dubbed the "SaaSpocalypse," targets every platform that bundles interface, logic, data, and workflow into one package sold per seat. Nearly all of scholarly publishing, from submission management systems to content databases, sits on top of platforms like this.

At the PurePub.ai event on May 22, 2026, Adam Hyde moderated as Hong Zhou of KnowledgeWorks Global, Stuart Rutch of Silverchair, and Paul Shannon of eLife took the question head-on. Asked whether agents amount to a full-scale assault on SaaS, the panel's answer was more interesting than a simple yes or no. Platforms aren't dying; they're splitting in two. Below, a trusted core; above, an agent layer. What used to connect the two — seats and screens — is letting go.

The split is happening because the consumer is changing. For thirty years, the platform's consumer was the person sitting in front of the screen — the seat. Now agents are standing alongside as consumers too, and at the next stage, regardless of who's doing the work, data passes through agents that talk directly to a headless core instead of a legacy interface. Rutch predicted platforms would "decompose into primitives." At the bottom sits a database loaded with business rules, and above it, "progressively, this agent layer" builds up — though who owns that layer is still undecided.

The interface used to hold trust and billing together. Familiarity — "the same interface you saw yesterday" — created trust, but once the interface detaches from the core and can be regenerated and swapped out at any time, that familiarity no longer vouches for what's underneath. Billing is even more serious. When a handful of people deploy agents, the load can't be measured by seat count. Hyde said he "doesn't think it's a seat model," and Rutch saw compute, not headcount, becoming the unit. Scenarios like per-token billing, outcome-based billing, and BYOK, where customers bring their own model API keys, also came up.

Still, the trust core remains. The cost of building in-house is falling thanks to AI coding agents, and systems opened up for agents to read make data migration just as easy, thinning both of SaaS's moats at once. But the verified records an institution has run and audited for years, its accumulated business logic, relationships, and industry knowledge, can't be replicated in a short time. Rutch sees "the trust dimension" remaining as the core system's essential value, and said he'd rather "disrupt ourselves at the same speed" before someone else does it first.

The panel's answer landed short of a full-scale assault. What's being challenged isn't the platform's existence but the assumption that it must be used only through a vendor-controlled interface and workflow. As agents come to mediate not just the discovery and consumption of research but also review, evaluation, production, and management, a growing share of value tilts toward the agent layer. Reading where value pools between the two layers becomes a core strategic task for publishers and vendors. Part two covers what happens once interfaces grow intelligent and personalized enough to break free of the platform.

Amazon will release a new Kindle lineup in late 2026. At the center of this lineup are a faster processor and more generous RAM. These specs are meant to run AI reading features on the device itself that go further than the existing Kindle Recap or “The Story So Far.”

The real point of interest isn't the hardware itself but the direction it points toward. It signals that on-device AI is moving deeply into how readers move through a book and look back at earlier content. AI recall and navigation features are now emerging as a key factor shaping Kindle specifications.
This is a notable item from a roundup of links for writers. OverDrive's Libby app now lets users filter out books that contain AI-generated content.

The filtering method is not automatic detection. It relies on labels that publishers and authors add themselves. The same roundup also included an Atlantic interview about a Commonwealth Prize winner accused of using AI.
As publishers weigh whether to add interactive 3D models to digital textbooks, generative AI is emerging as the lever that determines cost.
That's because draft 3D models can be generated from written descriptions or sketches alone. Before they reach the classroom, though, human experts still need to verify their accuracy.

A curated roundup of links for writers surfaced a UK legal analysis. Its diagnosis is that copyright law fails to adequately prevent the harm caused by AI training. It points to lawsuits collapsing on technical issues rather than on the merits.
The same issue also included an article on a wave of AI startups approaching publishers with tools for editing, rights, royalties, and recommendations.

A report by Millicent Weber of the Australian National University (ANU), 'Audiobook Listening in Australia,' surveyed 503 Australian listeners and 500 German listeners. Among them, 17.4% had already listened to an audiobook using AI narration or synthetic voice.
The perception gap is as notable as the listening habits themselves. Only 40% of Australians counted listening to audiobooks as 'reading.'
The full report and the remaining figures are only available to paying subscribers, so the details couldn't be confirmed.

At the International Publishers Association (IPA) congress in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, during the 'Emerging Markets: New Technology, New Challenges' session, moderator Fatima Abbas said, 'There is no single model for innovation.' She meant that because conditions differ from market to market, each one adopts new technology its own way.

Low King Hui, Group CEO of Malaysia's Sasbadi Holdings, said the industry has been going through a digital transition for nearly 20 years. He noted that making digital revenue work while sustaining investment remains difficult, and that AI is leveling the playing field, intensifying competition among existing publishers.

Ali Abdel-Moneim Ahmed, CEO of Egypt's Arabookers International, described using AI to track customers and competitors and to manage production. The company is rapidly scaling its business, partnering with Amazon and BookWire with a goal of digitizing 100,000 ebook titles and 1,000 audiobook titles.

GeumJoo Lin, co-founder and CEO of South Korea's CO.MINT, emphasized protecting copyright while expanding rights opportunities. In particular, she expressed concern that the trend of AI-generated books receiving legal deposit compensation from the National Library of Korea is eroding trust in publishing.

The YouTube channel 'AI Tool Box,' which covers AI software, reviewed 'Steamy Co-Author' hands-on. It describes the tool as AI writing software aimed at romance and genre fiction writers, built to help generate ideas, build characters, structure plots, and break through writer's block.

The video walks through the dashboard, story and character generation, the plot builder, dialogue and scene building, and pricing and add-on products (OTOs), in that order. It frames self-published authors who consistently publish through Kindle Direct Publishing (KDP) as the main target users.
That said, this review is a promotional video built around a WarriorPlus affiliate link and a bonus bundle, so its praise and criticism should be weighed with that in mind.

Baroness Thangam Debbonaire, a Labour peer and former Shadow Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport, spoke with The Bookseller after delivering the keynote at the Publishers' Licensing Services (PLS) conference. She described the creative industry's debate over AI as "a canary in the coal mine for a bigger question about the role of humans."

She directly pushes back on AI companies' argument that paying creators "doesn't add up." "It's basically telling creators, we're going to use your work but we're not going to compensate you for it," she said, adding, "if your business doesn't work when you pay people properly, then your business is wrong."

She also drew an analogy with construction. You need bricks, windows, a carpenter, and timber to build a house, and if you pay everyone else but refuse to pay the brick supplier and the carpenter, that isn't a legal business in this country.

She also raised concerns about depletion. Large language models use human writers' work as training data, and if that source disappears, "AI can't write new work." All that's left is repeating the same things, or AI training on AI.

Asked about the value of human creativity, she pointed to emotion. "We want human creativity because it moves us, soothes us, provokes us," she said. Even if AI could mimic that role, she asked, "then we have to ask the bigger philosophical question: isn't there something too important to being human to hand over entirely to AI?"

Licensing is a practical middle ground between fear and doing nothing. "It's better than having no licensing. There's no perfect system at this stage, but PLS is making a good start," she assessed. She favors fixing the current framework rather than overturning copyright law. She concluded, "if we carry on like this, we'll end up either running out of original creative work or having people work for free. Doing nothing is no longer an option."

According to Bunka News, Rakuten Books said at a strategy briefing for publishers in Tokyo on July 7 that it would reposition itself as a more "Rakuten-like" online bookstore. With 28 million monthly visitors, it ranks among the largest properties within the Rakuten marketplace.

Users are 57% women and 43% men, with housewives being the strongest segment among women's products. The company sees room to grow in categories aimed at men, like business books. 63% of users use both online and offline bookstores.

The new strategy has four prongs: promotion through the Rakuten ecosystem, keeping inventory stocked so no sales opportunity is missed, personalized discovery using Rakuten's data and AI, and benefits and experiences unique to Rakuten Books.

Outside Japan, Rakuten is mostly associated with Kobo and e-books, which tends to obscure the scale of its print book business. Rakuten Books is a major player going head-to-head with Amazon Japan in the print book market.

This op-ed, co-written by Cari Weaver and seven others, argues that a unified standard is needed for how AI use in research is disclosed. Just as funding sources or conflicts of interest are disclosed, AI use should be disclosed with the same rigor. "Transparently disclosing AI use is a matter of research integrity," the authors wrote.

There are many guidelines on responsible AI use, but there's no common standard for "how to disclose the way AI contributed to research findings." A 2026 survey found that about a third of researchers who use AI widely had never disclosed their AI use.

The World Conference on Research Integrity (WCRI) set up a focus track to close this gap. With support from groups including the International Science Council, it is refining a draft of the so-called "Vancouver Standard" through three rounds of consultation. The first round began in late 2025, the second in July 2026, and the third is scheduled for late 2026 to early 2027.

The first round of consultation showed a clear desire for standards, but also revealed tensions. The points of contention were how much detail to disclose, how to reconcile differing expectations across fields, and how to fit with existing frameworks.

The authors emphasize that the focus of disclosure is research integrity and the trustworthiness of methods. "Human responsibility and oversight remain central to using AI responsibly," and enough must be disclosed for a peer in the same field to judge whether AI's contribution affected the reliability of the results.

blocks.x: This report on Guatemala's book market covers CONTEC Guatemala's panel on “AI and Authorship.” Literary translators, publishers and authors gathered to discuss how translators might embrace AI tools.

They agreed that even as translators bring AI into their work, human translators remain indispensable. Literary translation means inventing a linguistic solution tailored to each text, which differs every time.

Debate went back and forth over how much could be handed to AI, but the conclusion leaned toward keeping humans in the seat of judgment. Guatemala's book market is growing, but it still faces familiar challenges.

In a survey commissioned by Spoken, an AI audiobook producer based in Portland, 61% of respondents mistook some AI narration for human voices. The same share viewed the use of AI voices favorably in scenes with multiple characters. In descriptive passages without multiple characters, though, they still preferred human narration.

The survey was conducted in May by Edison Research at SSRS among 1,005 US adults who identified as fiction audiobook listeners. Respondents randomly heard either a professional narrator's reading or an excerpt using Spoken's "Multi-Cast technology," which assigns a different voice to each character within a passage. Spoken markets the service as a cheaper, faster alternative to traditional productions that require coordinating multiple voice actors.

After hearing the sample, respondents who said they'd finish a multi-voice audiobook rose from 31% before listening to 65% after. Among frequent listeners, 81% expressed interest in different voices for different characters, and 51% said they were "very interested." Narration quality, immersion and multiple character voices mattered more to their choices than a low price or a celebrity narrator.

This announcement conflicts with a 2026 consumer survey that the Audio Publishers Association (APA) also commissioned from Edison. Released on June 5, that survey found willingness to try AI narration fell from 70% in 2025 to 61% in 2026, and only 16% of listeners had actually heard one. AI-narrated titles, despite rising in number, accounted for just 0.03% of audiobook sales in 2025.

"There's some demand for AI-generated narration, but our survey from a few months ago shows the share of listeners who've actually heard an AI-narrated audiobook is still pretty low," APA executive director Jim Dinegar told PW. He pointed to price sensitivity as one factor, noting that AI narration is growing for backlist titles or books with small markets because of recording costs.

Both studies were conducted by Edison, but their designs differed. Spoken measured reactions from a controlled, blind listening experiment, while the APA measured self-reported intentions from a broader listener base. Dialogue-heavy fiction, like stage drama, relies on emotional and psychological exchange between voices. A human narrator brings an interpretive, culturally inflected perspective to the text that even the most human-sounding AI isn't designed to replicate.

The conflicting surveys arrive amid a revival of interest in multi-voice production, which Audible recently showed with its full-cast audio edition of the complete Harry Potter series. Dinegar said the APA's sales survey confirmed "steady, impressive year-over-year growth in audiobook sales," but added, "listeners strongly prefer human voices."

Major publishers including Hachette, Cengage and Elsevier have filed suit against Google. They allege that Google used digital copies from Google Books, Google Play and Google Scholar to train its Gemini models without permission.
According to the complaint, Google's own internal review flagged the practice as "highly problematic" and warned of billions of dollars in potential fines, yet the company proceeded anyway.
It is a fight over rights and consent — whether book text may be used to train AI models, and if so, how it should be used.
The 35th International Publishers Association (IPA) Congress, held in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, wrapped up its two-day schedule on July 7. Three sessions addressed children's and YA publishing.

In the session "Connecting the World: Cross-Cultural Storytelling and Reading for the Next Generation," Canadian publishing consultant Simon de Jocas discussed the current state of children's literature and reading habits with Bologna Children's Book Fair director Elena Pasoli and Malaysian IBBY president Ahmad Redza bin Ahmad Khairuddin. Pasoli said, "Keep giving children what they love — usually the familiar and the known — but always introduce other things they need or should know," adding, "Books connect children who feel lonely to the world, letting them travel to other worlds and building a sense of belonging and empathy."

Ahmad Redza shared that he tried to pass on Enid Blyton's The Famous Five and The Secret Seven, books he cherished, to his children, but they showed no interest even in new editions, preferring The Lord of the Rings and Harry Potter instead. "The environment has changed, and children spend a lot of time at school. If they're still reading, that's enough, and it's hopeful," he said. He also stressed, "Technology is neither a threat nor an evil. Digital books give children who need special support access to content. The issue isn't format — it's content."

The session "Carrying On a Legacy: Half a Century of Children's Publishing" turned attention to Gallimard Jeunesse, one of the world's leading children's publishers. CEO Hedwige Pasquet sat down with Karine Pansa, CEO of Grupo Girassol Brasil. In 2025, backlist titles such as The Little Prince, Beatrix Potter, Harry Potter and Roald Dahl accounted for more than 64% of the company's total revenue of 52 million euros, with 6 million euros of that coming from sales abroad. One in every ten books sold to children and young people worldwide is a Gallimard Jeunesse book.

Pasquet said the company's goals and values have remained unchanged since its founding, citing outstanding content, beauty conveyed through illustration, and creativity in developing new formats. She said AI is used mainly for marketing and promotion, not in the editorial process.

On the Congress's second day, the deepening literacy crisis took center stage. Hundreds of millions of children and young people grow up without books. UNESCO Goodwill Ambassador for Education and Book Culture, and founder of Kalimat Group and PublisHer, Sheikha Bodour Al Qasimi spoke with Emma House of Oreham Group. She said, "Publications are abundant, but in refugee camps or places without internet, both print and e-books are hard to come by," adding, "With books, even refugees can redraw their path to the future."

She went on to say, "It's not books that make readers — it's a culture of reading that makes readers," adding, "AI is changing how books are made, but no algorithm falls in love with reading. People can. A single book changes a life."
